[[AFCA Coach of the Year]] (1943) | coaching_records = | CFBHOF_year = 1951 | BASKHOF_year = 1959 | CFBHOF_id = 2097 | BASKHOF_id = amos-alonzo-stagg }} '''Amos Alonzo Stagg''' (August 16, 1862 – March 17, 1965) was an American athlete and college coach in multiple sports, primarily [[American football]].{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=VQJPAAAAIBAJ&pg=7344%2C2868105 |work=Toledo Blade |location=Ohio |agency=wire service reports |title=Sport, not winning was Stagg's ultimate goal |date=March 18, 1965 |page=32}}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=XwBWAAAAIBAJ&pg=6506%2C4009177 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=...As long as 'football' is still called 'football' |date=March 18, 1965 |page=1D}} He introduced many innovations to American football. Stagg served as the head football coach at the International [[YMCA]] Training School (now called [[Springfield College]]) (1890–1891), the [[Chicago Maroons football|University of Chicago]] (1892–1932), and the [[Pacific Tigers football|College of the Pacific]] (1933–1946), compiling a career [[college football]] record of {{winpct|314|199|35|record=y}}. His undefeated [[Chicago Maroons football|Chicago Maroons]] teams of [[1905 Chicago Maroons football team|1905]] and [[1913 Chicago Maroons football team|1913]] were recognized as [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national champions]]. He was also the head [[Chicago Maroons men's basketball|basketball]] coach for one season at Chicago (1920–1921), and the Maroons' head [[baseball]] coach for twenty seasons (1893–1905, 1907–1913). At Chicago, Stagg also instituted an annual prep basketball tournament and track meet. Both drew the top high school teams and athletes from around the United States. Stagg played football as an [[End (gridiron football)|end]] at [[Yale Bulldogs football|Yale University]] and was selected to the first [[All-America college football team|All-America team]] in [[1889 All-America college football team|1889]]. He was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] as both a player and a coach in the charter class of 1951 and was the only individual honored in both roles until the 1990s. Influential in other sports, Stagg developed basketball as a five-player sport. This five-man concept allowed his 10- (later 11-) man football team the ability to compete with each other and to stay in shape over the winter. Stagg was elected to the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame|Basketball Hall of Fame]] in its first group of inductees in 1959, and was elected Fellow #71 in the National Academy of Kinesiology (formerly American Academy of Physical Education) in 1946.{{cite journal |last1=Cardinal |first1=Bradley J. |title=The National Academy of Kinesiology: Its founding, focus, and future |journal=Kinesiology Review |date=2022 |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=6–25 |doi=10.1123/kr.2021-0064}} Stagg also forged a bond between sports and religious faith early in his career that remained important to him for the rest of his life.{{cite web|url=https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/e/spcl/centcat/fac/facch06_01.html|title=Special Collections Research Center - Special Collections Research Center - The University of Chicago Library|website=www.lib.UChicago.edu|access-date=October 23, 2017}} ==Early years == Stagg was born in a poor [[Irish Americans|Irish]] neighborhood of [[West Orange, New Jersey]], and attended [[Phillips Exeter Academy]].{{Harvnb|Pope|1956|page=236}}{{cite news|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1965/03/18/106986870.pdf|title=STAGG DIES AT 102; DEAN OF COACHES; 76 Years in College Football -- On First All-America $TAGGDIESATt02; DEAN OF GOACHES Football's Patriarch Led College Teams 70 Years|work=The New York Times |access-date=October 23, 2017}}[[File:Yale1888.jpg|thumb|260px|left|Stagg (far left) on Yale's [[1888 Yale Bulldogs football team|1888]] team]] Stagg entered Yale University in 1884 and received his bachelor's degree in 1888. {{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} At Yale, Stagg was a [[pitcher]] on the baseball team. He declined the offers to play for six different professional baseball teams. Stagg played on Yale's [[1888 Yale Bulldogs football team|1888]] football team, and was an end on the first [[All-America college football team|All-America team]] in [[1889 All-America college football team|1889]]. He was very active in the Yale YMCA where he served as general secretary during his last two years.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} Stagg spent two additional years at [[Yale Divinity School]], studying under [[William Rainey Harper]] before deciding he could have more influence on young men through coaching than through the pulpit. {{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} From 1890-1892, Stagg was an instructor at the International YMCA Training School, now known as [[Springfield College]], where teacher [[James Naismith]] had invented basketball in 1891.{{Harvnb|Lester|1995|page=9}} On March 11, 1892, Stagg, still an instructor at the YMCA School, played in the first public game of basketball. A crowd of 200 watched as the student team defeated the faculty, 5–1. Stagg scored the only basket for the losing side. He popularized the five-player lineup on basketball teams.[http://www.hoophall.com/hall-of-famers/tag/amos-alonzo-stagg Amos Alonzo Stagg] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090831070143/http://www.hoophall.com/hall-of-famers/tag/amos-alonzo-stagg |date=August 31, 2009 }} ==Coaching career== [[File:AAStagg-1906.jpg|thumb|left|Stagg in 1906.]] Stagg became the first paid football coach at [[Williston Northampton School|Williston Seminary]], a [[secondary school]], in 1890. This was also Stagg's first time receiving pay to coach football. He coached there one day a week while also coaching full-time at the International YMCA Training School.{{Harvnb|Considine|1962|page=37}} Stagg then coached at the [[University of Chicago]] from 1892 to 1932.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=7zxfAAAAIBAJ&pg=3170%2C9073092 |work=Youngstown Vindicator |location=Ohio |agency=Associated Press |last=Newland |first=Russ |title=She is "first lady of football!" |date=November 29, 1942 |page=D4}} He was the head football coach and director of the Department of Physical Culture.Shprintzen, Adam D. (2013). ''The Vegetarian Crusade: The Rise of an American Reform Movement, 1817-1921''. University of North Carolina Press. p. 199. {{ISBN|978-1-4696-0891-4}} Eventually, university president [[Robert Maynard Hutchins]] forced out the 70-year-old Stagg, feeling that he was too old to continue coaching.{{Harvnb|Davis|2006|page=135}}{{cite news |title=Stagg Is Retired As Chicago Coach |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1932/10/14/archives/stagg-is-retired-as-chicago-coach-university-invokes-age-rule-of-70.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=October 14, 1932 |access-date=October 25, 2010 }} At age 70, Stagg moved on to the [[University of the Pacific (United States)|College of the Pacific]] in [[Stockton, California]], where he led the [[Pacific Tigers football|Tigers]] for 14 seasons, from 1933 through 1946, then was asked to resign.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=k6IzAAAAIBAJ&dq=pacific%20football&pg=2745%2C5743369|title=COP, Stagg still confer|date=December 3, 1946|work=Lodi News-Sentinel|location=California|agency=United Press |page=12}} One of his players at Pacific in 1945-46 was [[Wayne Hardin]], who later became the Hall of Fame coach of Navy and Temple. In the [[1924 Summer Olympics]] in [[Paris]], Stagg served as a coach with the [[United States at the 1924 Summer Olympics#Athletics|U.S. Olympic Track and Field team]]. He played himself in the movie ''[[Knute Rockne, All American]]'', released in 1940. From 1947 to 1952 he served as co-coach with his son, [[Amos Alonzo Stagg, Jr.|Amos Jr.]], at [[Susquehanna University]] in Pennsylvania. Stagg's final job was as kicking coach at the local junior college in Stockton, California, which was then known as [[San Joaquin Delta College|Stockton College]]. "The Grand Old Man of Football" retired from Stockton College at the age of 96 and died in Stockton six years later.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=PmkzAAAAIBAJ&pg=7073%2C5234838 |work=Lodi News Sentinel |location=California |last=Kretzer |first=Dale |title=Last whistle blows for famous coach |date=March 18, 1965 |page=1}} ===Vegetarianism=== Stagg was reportedly an activist for [[vegetarianism]] and banned his players from using alcohol and tobacco.Mcthenia, Tal. (2018). [https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/athletes-who-are-vegetarian "How a Football Team Became Mascots for Vegetarianism"]. Atlasobscura.com. Retrieved 6 October 2021. In 1907, he trained his Chicago football team on a strict vegetarian diet. This was widely reported in newspapers and vegetarian literature.[https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn84023416/1907-10-18/ed-1/seq-1/ "Vegetable Football"]. ''Essex County Herald'' (October 18, 1907).[https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn87056244/1907-10-03/ed-1/seq-2/ "Vegetarianism in Football"]. ''The Plymouth Tribune'' (October 03, 1907).[https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015074774673&view=1up&seq=6 "Vegetarianism and Football"]. ''The Vegetarian and Our Fellow Creatures'' 11, no. 6 (October 1907): 4; [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015074774673&view=1up&seq=8 "Vegetarian Diet for the Chicago University Football Team"]. ''The Vegetarian and Our Fellow Creatures'' 11, no. 6 (October 1907): 6. Stagg had spent time at the vegetarian [[Battle Creek Sanitarium]] in 1907 and was inspired by [[John Harvey Kellogg]]'s vegetarian diet. Although Stagg was cited in vegetarian literature as advocating a strict vegetarian diet throughout his life, in his memoir he stated that he was a vegetarian for only two years and did it in an attempt to relieve his chronic [[Sciatic nerve|sciatic]] pain. Stagg did not consume alcohol, coffee, or cigarettes and promoted the consumption of vegetables over red meat. ==Family and personal life== [[File:Amos Alonzo Stagg 1899 UC yearbook.png|thumb|left|170px|Stagg in 1899]] Stagg was married to the former Stella Robertson on September 10, 1894. The couple had three children: two sons, [[Amos Alonzo Stagg Jr.|Amos Jr.]] and [[Paul Stagg|Paul]], and a daughter, Ruth. Both sons played for the elder Stagg as [[quarterback]]s at the University of Chicago and each later coached college football. In 1952, Barbara Stagg, Amos' granddaughter, started coaching the high school girls' [[basketball]] team for [[Northern Lehigh High School]] in [[Slatington, Pennsylvania]]. In 1933, Stagg donated an [[Milburn Light Electric]] 1921 Model 27L Brougham automobile (of which he was the original owner) to Chicago's [[Museum of Science and Industry (Chicago)|Museum of Science & Industry]]. The vehicle remains in the museum's collection, and is today own of only 56 known surviving Milburn Light Electric vehicles in world.{{cite web |title=Registry |url=http://www.milburn.us/registry.htm |website=Milburn.us |access-date=26 March 2026}} ==Legacy== Two high schools in the United States, [[Amos Alonzo Stagg High School|one]] in [[Palos Hills, Illinois]], and the [[Stagg High School (Stockton, California)|other]] in [[Stockton, California]], and an elementary school in [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]], are named after Stagg.{{cite web|url=http://www.cps.edu/Schools/Pages/school.aspx?unit=7760|title=CPS : Schools : School|website=www.CPS.edu|access-date=October 23, 2017}}{{cite web|url=https://district.d230.org/stagg/default.aspx|title=Home Page - Stagg|website=district.d230.org|access-date=October 23, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130701211945/https://district.d230.org/stagg/default.aspx|archive-date=July 1, 2013|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=http://ashs-susd-ca.schoolloop.com/|title=School Loop: Participating Schools|website=ashs-susd-ca.SchoolLoop.com|access-date=October 23, 2017}} The [[NCAA Division III National Football Championship]] game, played in [[Salem, Virginia]], is named the Stagg Bowl after him. The athletic stadium at [[Springfield College]] is named [[Stagg Field (Springfield College)|Stagg Field]].{{cite web|title=Stagg Field |url=http://www.spfldcol.edu/homepage/athletics.nsf/FootballHeadlineHomePage |access-date=November 17, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111105050626/http://www.spfldcol.edu/homepage/athletics.nsf/FootballHeadlineHomePage |archive-date=November 5, 2011 }} The football field at [[Susquehanna University]] is named Amos Alonzo Stagg Field in honor of both Stagg Sr. and Jr.{{cite web | title=Amos Alonzo Stagg Field at Nicholas A. Lopardo Stadium| work=Susquehanna| url=http://www.gosusqu.com/information/facilities/amos-alonzo-stagg-field-at-nicholas-a-lopardo-stadium| access-date=November 17, 2011}} Stagg was also the namesake of the University of Chicago's old [[Stagg Field]].{{cite web| title=The Manhattan Project| url=http://physics.uchicago.edu/about/history/manhattan.html| access-date=November 17, 2011| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111028100736/http://physics.uchicago.edu/about/history/manhattan.html| archive-date=October 28, 2011| df=mdy-all}} At [[University of the Pacific (United States)|University of the Pacific]] in [[Stockton, California]], one of the campus streets is known as Stagg Way and Pacific Memorial Stadium, the school's football and soccer stadium, was renamed [[Stagg Memorial Stadium|Amos Alonzo Stagg Memorial Stadium]] on October 15, 1988.{{cite web| title=Stagg Memorial Stadium| url=http://pacifictigers.cstv.com/facilities/paci-stagg.html| access-date=November 17, 2011| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080825090709/http://pacifictigers.cstv.com/facilities/paci-stagg.html| archive-date=August 25, 2008| url-status=dead}} [[Phillips Exeter Academy]] also has a field named for him and a statue.{{cite web | title=Athletic and Outdoor Facilities| url=http://www.exeter.edu/about_us/171_239.aspx| access-date=November 17, 2011}} A field in [[West Orange, New Jersey]] on Saint Cloud Avenue is also named for him.{{cite web|url=http://www.westorange.org/index.asp?Type=B_BASIC&SEC=%7B44256A3D-05D0-4C88-A07F-BBAFA44333B2%7D&DE=%7BF9BFA053-CF4A-42F6-A305-7FCC82944BF3%7D|title=West Orange, NJ - Official Website|website=www.WestOrange.org|access-date=October 23, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928225919/http://www.westorange.org/index.asp?Type=B_BASIC&SEC=%7B44256A3D-05D0-4C88-A07F-BBAFA44333B2%7D&DE=%7BF9BFA053-CF4A-42F6-A305-7FCC82944BF3%7D|archive-date=September 28, 2011|url-status=dead}} The [[Amos Alonzo Stagg Award]] is awarded annually to the "individual, group, or institution whose services have been outstanding in the advancement of the best interests of football." The winner of the [[Big Ten Football Championship Game]], started in 2011, receives the [[Stagg Championship Trophy]], named in his honor.{{cite news | agency=Associated Press |title=Big Ten removes Joe Paterno's name from championship trophy |publisher=The Detroit News |date=November 14, 2011}} At the [[College of William and Mary]], the Amos Alonzo Stagg Society was organized during 1979–1980 by students and faculty opposed to a plan by the institution's Board of Visitors to move William and Mary back into big-time college football several decades after a scandal there involving grade changes for football players. The Society was loosely organized but successful in combating, among other plans, a major expansion of the William and Mary football stadium. [[File:Amos stagg and plaque.jpg|thumb|Stagg in 1962]] Collections of Amos Alonzo Stagg's papers are held at the University of Chicago Library, Special Collections Research Center and at the University of the Pacific Library, Holt Atherton Department of Special Collections.{{cite web | title=Guide to the Amos Alonzo Stagg Papers 1866-1964| url=https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/e/scrc/findingaids/view.php?eadid=ICU.SPCL.STAGG| access-date=July 16, 2013}}{{cite web | title=Amos Alonzo Stagg Collection| url=http://cdn.calisphere.org/data/13030/05/tf5489p105/files/tf5489p105.pdf| access-date=November 17, 2011}} The Alonzo Stagg 50/20 Hike goes through [[Arlington, Virginia]], [[Washington, DC]] and [[Maryland]].{{cite web|url=http://troop111.org/activities/alonzo-stagg-5020-hike/|title=Alonzo Stagg 50/20 Hike - BSA Troop 111 Arlington, Virginia|website=Troop111.org|date=May 14, 2011 |access-date=October 23, 2017}} The [[Stagg (tree)|Stagg Tree]], a giant sequoia in the [[Alder Creek Grove]] and the fifth largest tree in the world, is named in honor of Amos Alonzo Stagg. Stagg is also an elected Fellow in the National Academy of Kinesiology (née the American Academy of Physical Education). ===Stagg Bowl=== The Amos Alonzo Stagg Bowl, otherwise known as the [[NCAA Division III Football Championship]] Game since 1973, is competed annually as the final game of the NCAA Division III Football Tournament. The Stagg Bowl can be traced back to 1969, prior to the inception of the D-III national championship. At that time—from 1969 to 1973—the Stagg Bowl was one of two bowls competed at the College Division level—the [[Knute Rockne Bowl]] and the Amos Alonzo Stagg Bowl. In 1973, the NCAA instituted the D-III national championship, and the Stagg Bowl was adopted as the moniker for that game. The first 10 Stagg Bowls were played in Phenix City, Alabama, from 1973 to 1982. Wittenberg University (Ohio) won the inaugural game via a 41–0 result over Juniata College (Pa.). The game moved to Kings Island, Ohio, for the 1983 and 1984 editions, with Augustana College (Ill.) winning the first two of its four straight NCAA titles. The Stagg Bowl returned to Phenix City for five more years, before spending three seasons in Bradenton, Florida. In 1993, the Stagg Bowl moved to Salem, Va., where it remained until 2017.{{cite web |last=Popovich |first=Mike |date=October 15, 2020 |title=Tom Benson Hall of Stadium awarded 2025 Amos Alonzo Stagg Bowl |url=https://www.cantonrep.com/story/sports/college/football/2020/10/14/tom-benson-hall-stadium-awarded-2025-amos-alonzo-stagg-bowl/3659751001/ |access-date=September 1, 2026 |website=The Repository}} The [[University of Mount Union]] (formerly Mount Union College) won the first of its NCAA Division III-record 13 football national championships in 1993.NCAA Division III Football Championship record book The Championship was held in Shenandoah, TX, in 2018 and 2019. [[Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium]] at Hall of Fame Village powered by [[Johnson Controls]] in [[Canton, Ohio]], was originally awarded the 2020 and 2021 Stagg Bowls; however, the 2020 Championship was cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The 2021 Stagg Bowl was held at [[Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium]] December 2–4, 2021.{{Cite web|url=https://www.visitcanton.com/events-calendar/ohsaa-state-football-championships/|title = Ohio High School Football Championship}} [[Navy–Marine Corps Memorial Stadium]] in [[Annapolis, Maryland]] hosted the 2022 Stagg Bowl,{{Cite web |title=2022 NCAA Division III football championship field announced {{!}} NCAA.com |url=https://www.ncaa.com/news/football/article/2022-11-13/2022-ncaa-division-iii-football-championship-field-announced |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=www.ncaa.com |language=en}} where [[North Central College]] defeated [[University of Mount Union]]. In 2023, [[Salem Football Stadium]] in [[Salem, Virginia]] was awarded the game. ===Innovations=== The following is a list of innovations Stagg introduced to American football. Where known, the year of its first use is annotated in parentheses. Stagg is noted as a 'contributor' if he was one of a group of individuals responsible for a given innovation.
